title: Providence follows the mind
hookLine: he teaches that providence follows how closely the mind is joined to God
carry: for maimonides, god's care follows the turned mind

cards: A leaf lets go of a branch and drifts down. A spider in the corner of a window catches a fly. Did God decide that this leaf would fall at this moment, and that this fly would be the one?
Maimonides raises exactly these examples in the Guide, and his answer is blunt. No, he says. Not for the leaf, not for the fly.
Then he turns to human beings, and his answer changes, but with a condition attached.

teach.h: THE LEAF: THE SPECIES IS WATCHED.
teach.b: Providence follows attention. Providence means God's care and guidance over what happens. First, the leaf.

In the third part of the Guide, Maimonides says that for plants and animals, God's providence watches over the species, not each individual. The falling leaf and the caught fly happen by the ordinary workings of nature.
Second, the person. With human beings it's different.

teach.h: THE PERSON: CARE FOLLOWS THE MIND.
teach.b: Providence over a person follows the divine overflow that reaches them, and that depends on their mind: the more a person's intellect is joined to God, the closer the care. It isn't handed out equally, like rain.

teach.h: THE PALACE, AND A WANDERING MIND.
teach.b: Third, the palace. Near the end of the Guide, he tells a parable of a king in his palace and people at different distances from him, some still outside the walls, some in the inner rooms.
And he adds a sharp point: when a person's mind is fully elsewhere, busy with other things, in that hour the bond is loosened.
He reads the Psalm this way: "Because he hath set his love upon Me, therefore will I deliver him." Fourth, the other voices. This was a bold view, and not everyone held it.
Later teachers, among them Hasidic masters, taught that God's care reaches every detail, and tradition says the Baal Shem Tov held that even a leaf turns in the wind by providence.
Both views are still taught. Maimonides' version makes care something a person can move toward: turn the mind toward God, and keep it turned.

how: Jewish teaching values kavanah, focused intention, in prayer and in keeping the commandments. Students of the Guide study Maimonides' view of providence in its third part, often alongside Hasidic teachings that God's care reaches every detail.

games.q: you're Maimonides. a student asks whether God decided which fly the spider would catch. what do you say?
o: no; for animals, providence watches the species.
nobody can say anything about it.
games.why: he says the spider and the fly are nature's ordinary workings. individual providence, for him, is for human beings, and follows the mind.

practice: Give one thing your full attention: your breath, a single sound in the room, or, if you pray, one line of a prayer you know.
When your mind wanders off to the day, notice it, the way Maimonides noticed the mind leaving the palace, and come back with no scolding. Each return is the practice.

wordCard.voice: Providence follows attention. Maimonides' teaching that God's care over a person grows with how closely their mind is turned to God, and loosens when the mind turns away. Today's word.
